name: Didibri
description: Didibri are dragon-like creatures from Surinamese folklore, derived from the Sranan Tongo word for devil or dragon. These fearsome beings appear in the oral traditions of Suriname's diverse population, including Creole, Maroon, and Indigenous communities. The most famous tale, documented by folklorists Melville and Frances Herskovits in the early 20th century, tells of a twelve-tailed dragon named Didibri who transforms himself into a handsome human — calling himself Je Man — to woo a human woman. His twelve dragon brothers await to devour her. The story features magical objects called obia that the woman's brother uses to create obstacles — a great lake, a sea of fire, a field of cutting grass, and a mountain — that the dragons must overcome. Didibri represents the boundary between the human world and the dangerous spiritual realm in Surinamese cosmology
source: Surinamese Winti folklore — Didibri dragon-like spirit.

name: Curse of Dido (Carthaginian Curse)
description: The Curse of Dido (also known as the Carthaginian Curse) is one of the most enduring legends in Tunisian folklore. According to the myth, when the Roman Republic destroyed Carthage in 146 BC, the spirit of Queen Dido (also known as Elissa), the legendary founder of Carthage, placed a curse on the city's ruins. The curse proclaimed that no city would ever prosper on the site where Carthage once stood. Dido was a Phoenician princess who, according to tradition, founded Carthage in 814 BC after fleeing her murderous brother Pygmalion. The legend holds that Dido's spirit has haunted the site ever since, preventing any permanent settlement or development from thriving there. This explains why the ruins of Carthage, despite being a UNESCO World Heritage site and located in one of the most desirable coastal areas of Tunisia, remain largely undeveloped and uninhabited. The curse is said to manifest through unexplained phenomena, and locals report hearing Dido's lament carried on the wind. The story has become a symbol of Tunisian cultural resistance and the power of the ancient past over the present
source: Carthage Magazine; Tunisian oral traditions

name: Dievas
description: Dievas is the primordial supreme sky god in Baltic mythology, worshipped by ancient Lithuanians, Latvians, and Old Prussians as the creator of the universe and ruler of all deities. His name derives from the Proto-Indo-European sky father *Dyēus, making him cognate with the Vedic Dyaus Pita, Greek Zeus, and Roman Jupiter. Dievas is the god of light, sky, prosperity, and wealth, and alongside Perkūnas (thunder god) and Potrimpo, forms the supreme triad of Baltic deities. According to creation myths, Dievas and his twin brother Velns, the trickster god, created the universe by wrestling upon a rock in the primordial ocean, which became the center of the world. He is also known as Praamžius, the god of time, sky, peace, and friendship. His two sons, the Ašvieniai, are the divine twins who pull the sun goddess Saulė's chariot across the sky
source: Baltic mythology; Dievas is the supreme sky god and creator.

name: Dilyéhé (Mountain Sheep People)
description: Dilyéhé, known as the Mountain Sheep People, are sacred animal-spirit beings in Navajo (Diné) tradition who serve as the guardians of the mountains. They are among the Holy People who taught the Navajo people how to live in harmony with the natural world. The Mountain Sheep People possess deep knowledge of the high country — its plants, waters, and paths — and they share this wisdom with humans who approach them with proper respect and offerings. They grant blessings of health, hunting success, and protection during mountain travel. In Navajo cosmology, the Dilyéhé inhabit a realm between the physical and spiritual worlds, appearing in visions and ceremonies to those who seek their guidance. They are closely associated with the sacred mountains that define the four cardinal boundaries of Dinétah, the traditional Navajo homeland
source: Navajo (Diné) spiritual tradition; documented in Southwestern ethnographic records.

name: Diser
description: The Diser (singular: Dis, from Old Norse dís meaning "lady") are a collective of powerful female spirits in Norse mythology and Germanic tradition who act as protective guardians of individuals, families, and clans. They are intimately associated with fate, fertility, and death, occupying a mysterious space between deities, ancestral spirits, and supernatural guardians. The Disir encompass a broad range of female supernatural figures including valkyries (called "Odin's Disir"), norns, and certain goddesses like Freyja. They could be either benevolent protectors who guided their charges through life or harbingers of doom whose appearance foretold death. The dísablót, a major sacrificial festival held at the beginning of winter, was dedicated to the Disir, and the Disting fair in Uppsala still carries their name today. In Swedish folklore, they were believed to be the spirits of female ancestors who watched over their descendants, and offerings were made to them at births, weddings, and funerals
source: Poetic Edda, Prose Edda, Icelandic sagas

name: Div-e Sepid
description: Div-e Sepid, the White Demon, is a legendary creature from Persian and Afghan mythology, best known as the chieftain of the divs of Mazandaran and the penultimate adversary in Rostam's Seven Labors from Ferdowsi's Shahnameh. The White Demon is a being of colossal size and power, commanding armies of lesser divs from his cave fortress in the mountains. He is described as having white skin or fur, a black face, and immense strength. His most devastating power is his ability to blind entire armies through sorcery — he destroys Kay Kavus's forces by conjuring a dark storm of hail, boulders, and tree trunks, then captures the king and his paladins, blinds them, and imprisons them in a dungeon. Only Rostam can defeat him, extracting the White Demon's liver to restore sight to the blinded heroes. Some scholars interpret the White Demon as a symbolic representation of Zal, Rostam's albino father, making their battle an Oedipal struggle
source: Persian epic mythology — Div-e Sepid (White Demon) from Ferdowsi's Shahnameh.

name: Div (Daeva)
description: Div (Daeva) is a demon from Afghanistan mythology. Their mythology draws from both Zoroastrian and pre-Islamic traditions, blending with local Afghan beliefs about supernatural entities. In Afghan folk tales collected from the Hindu Kush to the Helmand Valley, divs appear as malevolent spirits who guard hidden treasures, kidnap travelers, and terrorize mountain villages. Unlike their Persian counterparts, Afghan divs are more closely tied to specific geographical landmarks — particular peaks, springs, and caves are known as div-dwellings. The folklore of Pashtun and Tajik communities includes stories of heroes who must outwit or overpower these divs to rescue captives or claim treasure. The divs of Afghan tradition reflect the harsh landscape they inhabit, embodying the dangers of the wilderness beyond village boundaries
source: Persianate Afghan folklore — Div/Daeva demonic figures.

name: Div (Daeva)
description: Div (Daeva) in Afghan and Central Asian Persian folklore are demonic beings who inhabit the rugged mountains, remote deserts, and deep caves of the region. Their mythology draws from both Zoroastrian and pre-Islamic traditions, blending with local Afghan beliefs about supernatural entities. In Afghan folk tales collected from the Hindu Kush to the Helmand Valley, divs appear as malevolent spirits who guard hidden treasures, kidnap travelers, and terrorize mountain villages. Unlike their Persian counterparts, Afghan divs are more closely tied to specific geographical landmarks — particular peaks, springs, and caves are known as div-dwellings. The folklore of Pashtun and Tajik communities includes stories of heroes who must outwit or overpower these divs to rescue captives or claim treasure. The divs of Afghan tradition reflect the harsh landscape they inhabit, embodying the dangers of the wilderness beyond village boundaries
source: Persian mythology — Div/Daeva demonic figures in Persian tradition.

name: Dokkaebi
description: Dokkaebi are legendary goblin-like creatures from Korean mythology and folklore, deeply embedded in both North and South Korean cultural traditions. Unlike ghosts (gwishin), dokkaebi are nature deities or spirits born from inanimate objects that have been imbued with spiritual energy over time — old discarded household tools like brooms, farming implements, or objects stained with human blood and emotions. They possess extraordinary supernatural powers and are known for their mischievous and unpredictable interactions with humans. Dokkaebi are neither purely good nor evil; they reward kindness and punish greed, often testing human morality through games and challenges. They are famously associated with the dokkaebi bangmangi, a magical club that can grant wishes and summon objects, though it cannot create life. Dokkaebi are skilled at ssireum (Korean wrestling) and cannot be beaten unless their right side is exploited. They are strongly attracted to buckwheat products and can be warded off by horse blood or sieves hung outside doors In North Korea folklore, this figure is known among the North Korea people.
source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tokkaebi / https://www.britannica.com/topic/dokkaebi / National Folk Museum of Korea

source: Korean folklore; Dokkaebi are mischievous goblin spirits.

name: Domovoi
description: The Domovoi is a household spirit in Russian and Slavic folklore, deeply rooted in pre-Christian ancestor worship traditions. The name comes from the Russian 'dom' meaning house — the Domovoi is literally 'the one of the household.' This spirit lives behind the stove, under the threshold, or in the attic of traditional Slavic homes, serving as the guardian of the family. Belief in the Domovoi has persisted for centuries, surviving Christianization and continuing into modern times, particularly in rural areas. The Domovoi is considered the personification of the family's founder or a deceased male ancestor, making it an integral part of ancestor veneration. When a family moves to a new home, they perform a ritual to invite the Domovoi to join them, often by leaving bread and salt as offerings. The spirit ensures domestic harmony, protects children and livestock, and maintains the moral order of the household. Neglecting the Domovoi or behaving immorally causes it to become angry and potentially abandon the home, leaving the family vulnerable to misfortune
source: Slavic folklore, collected by Alexander Afanasyev

name: Domovoy
description: The Domovoy is the protective household spirit of Slavic mythology, worshipped across Russia, Ukraine, Belarus, Poland, Serbia, and other Slavic nations. Derived from the Proto-Slavic root 'dom' meaning house, the Domovoy is the master and guardian of the home who protects the family from harm, oversees domestic harmony, and ensures the prosperity of the household. According to folklorist E. Kagarov, the Domovoy is a personification of the supreme god Rod in the microcosm of the family. The Domovoy is closely linked to ancestor worship — many traditions identify the spirit as the soul of the family's founder or a deceased male relative. The Domovoy has a female counterpart called Domania, Kikimora, or Domovikha who handles the domestic sphere. Unlike many European household spirits, the Domovoy is deeply integrated into the religious and moral life of the family, not merely a mischievous sprite but a guardian of the kin's spiritual and physical well-being
source: Slavic folklore, collected by Alexander Afanasyev

name: Domovoy (Slavic House Spirit)
description: The Domovoy, known as Domovoi or Domovik in various Slavic languages, is a household spirit deeply rooted in Slavic mythology across Russia, Ukraine, Belarus, Poland, Serbia, and other Eastern European nations. The name derives from the Proto-Slavic root 'dom' meaning house, establishing this entity as the master and guardian of the home who protects the family and oversees domestic harmony. According to folklorist E. Kagarov, the Domovoy represents a personification of the supreme god Rod within the microcosm of the family, linking it directly to ancestral worship traditions where the soul of the family's founder continues to watch over the living. The Domovoy is deeply integrated into the moral framework of the household, not merely as a mischievous sprite but as a guardian of the kin's physical and spiritual well-being across all aspects of domestic life
source: Slavic folklore, collected by Alexander Afanasyev

name: Doña Sebastiana
description: Doña Sebastiana is a folk figure from New Mexican Hispano culture, depicted as a skeleton riding a wooden cart or chariot, carrying a bow and arrow. She is the northern New Mexican variant of the Grim Reaper, brought by Spanish colonists and merged with Indigenous death imagery. Unlike the anonymous European Death, Doña Sebastiana has a name and personality — she is said to be vengeful toward sinners but merciful to the faithful. Her image appears in the santero tradition of New Mexican folk art, particularly in the bultos (wooden carvings) of the penitentes. In some stories, she is the same figure as Santa Muerte; snip in others, a separate entity — a skeletal woman who appears to those about to die, giving them a final chance to confess their sins. Her cart is said to be heard rattling through the mountain villages of northern New Mexico on the night before someone dies. Doña Sebastiana represents the unique religious synthesis of Spanish Catholicism and Puebloan spirituality that characterizes the Hispano culture of New Mexico, a tradition that has endured for over 400 years
source: Pueblo spiritual tradition; documented in Southwestern ethnographic records.

name: Douen
description: The Domovoy, known as Domovoi or Domovik in various Slavic languages, is a household spirit deeply rooted in Slavic mythology across Russia, Ukraine, Belarus, Poland, Serbia, and other Eastern European nations. The name derives from the Proto-Slavic root 'dom' meaning house, establishing this entity as the master and guardian of the home who protects the family, oversees domestic harmony, and ensures household prosperity. According to folklorist E. Kagarov, the Domovoy represents a personification of the supreme god Rod within the microcosm of the family, linking it directly to ancestral worship traditions where the soul of the family's founder or a deceased male relative continues to watch over the living. The Domovoy shares a strong connection with the hearth and is deeply integrated into the moral framework of the household, not merely as a mischievous sprite but as a guardian of the kin's physical and spiritual well-being
source: Trinidadian folklore — Douen are forest spirits documented in Trinidadian oral tradition.

name: Dovregubben
description: Dovregubben (The Dovre King/Old Man of Dovre) is the king of the trolls who lives in the Dovre Mountains, created by Norwegian playwright Henrik Ibsen for his 1867 play Peer Gynt. Dovregubben is a huge, ugly troll king with a nose like a club and a scepter made of a cow's tail. In Peer Gynt, he presides over his troll court in the Dovre Hall and gives Peer the infamous ultimatum: "Be true to yourself, enough for yourself" (the troll's motto, contrasting with the human ideal of "be yourself"). The phrase "I Dovregubbens hall" (In the Hall of the Mountain King) was immortalized by Edvard Grieg's famous musical composition. Though created by Ibsen, Dovregubben has become deeply embedded in Norwegian folklore as the quintessential troll king. The Dovre Mountains themselves have been associated with trolls since medieval times
source: Scandinavian folklore; trolls are pervasive anthropomorphic beings in Nordic myths, documented in laestadian and ethnographic records.

name: Drac
description: The Douen, also spelled Dwen in Saint Lucian folklore, is a feared entity from Trinidadian and Tobagonian folklore with roots in African, French, Spanish, and English cultural influences. These are the spirits of unbaptized children who died before receiving Christian baptism, condemning them to wander the earth rather than finding peace in the afterlife. The Douen are most commonly found in dense forests and woodlands across Trinidad and the wider Caribbean, where they use their ability to mimic the voices of parents and loved ones to lure children away from safety and deep into the wilderness. Their primary purpose is to lead travelers and especially children astray until they become hopelessly lost, and they are considered one of the most dangerous folklore entities in the region, used by parents for generations to teach children the importance of staying close to home and the dangers of wandering alone
source: Catalan folklore — Drac dragon documented in Catalan oral tradition.

name: Drache
description: The Drac is a dragon-like creature from French folklore, particularly associated with the Provence region and southern France, where legends describe it as a shapeshifting water dragon that inhabits rivers, lakes, and coastal waters. Unlike the typical winged dragons of northern European tradition, the Drac is often depicted as wingless but possessing multiple legs, a long serpentine body, and the ability to transform into human form at will. In Provencal folklore, the Drac is known for its complex relationship with humans, sometimes demanding tribute from villages in the form of livestock or even human sacrifices, while at other times forming unexpected alliances with shepherds and farmers. The creature is deeply woven into the fabric of French medieval bestiaries and continues to appear in regional folklore throughout the country, where it represents the dangerous yet sometimes benevolent forces of nature that dwell in the waterways of the French countryside
source: Germanic folklore — Drache dragon documented in German oral tradition.

name: Naga Berani (Dragon of Brunei Bay)
description: Naga Berani (The Brave Dragon) is a legendary sea dragon said to inhabit the waters of Brunei Bay, a large, sheltered bay on the northern coast of Borneo. According to Bruneian folklore, this massive naga was once a celestial guardian that descended to protect the waters of Brunei. Its serpentine body is said to be so long that it can coil around the entire bay, and its scales shimmer with the colors of the sunset reflecting off the water. The dragon controls the tides, protects fishermen from storms, and guides ships safely to harbor. In some tales, it is the guardian of a sunken kingdom beneath Brunei Bay — a once-great city that was swallowed by the sea as punishment for its inhabitants' arrogance. The dragon surfaces only during times of great significance for the nation, appearing as a line of shimmering waves or a mysterious wake in the bay's waters
source: Bruneian coastal Malay folklore — the dragon of Brunei Bay.

name: Drakaina
description: The Drache is the German term for dragon, encompassing a rich tradition of dragon mythology that spans Germanic folklore from the medieval period through modern times. In German legend, the Drache is typically depicted as a massive, fire-breathing reptile that dwells in remote mountainous regions, deep caves, and dark forests, where it guards immense hoards of treasure accumulated over centuries. The Drache occupies a central role in Germanic heroic sagas and folktales, most notably in the Nibelungenlied where the hero Siegfried famously slays the dragon Fafnir and bathes in its blood to gain invulnerability. Across the German-speaking lands, countless regional variations of the Drache legend exist, from the Lindwurm of the Alps to the winged dragons of the northern lowlands, each reflecting local beliefs about these powerful creatures that test the courage and cunning of heroes while serving as guardians of ancient secrets and forbidden knowledge
source: Greek mythology — Drakaina female serpent/dragon documented in Greek mythology.

name: Drake (Swedish)
description: In Swedish folklore, the drake is a wingless, serpentine dragon that guards treasure hoards deep in the forest. Unlike the fire-breathing dragons of continental European legend, the Swedish drake is primarily a giant serpent with a horse-like mane or fish-like dorsal fin along its spine. It is often called lindorm (lindworm) and is distinguished by its ability to make treasure grow: anything lying beneath a drake increases in value at the same rate the serpent grows. The drake can spit a foul milk-like substance that blinds its enemies, and when threatened it may swallow its own tail to form a wheel and roll away at high speed, earning it the nickname hjulorm (wheel snake). Drake eggs are said to be laid under linden trees, and once hatched the young slither away to make homes in piles of rocks. The belief in drakes survived long after Christianization and persisted well into the 19th century in rural Sweden
source: Swedish folklore

name: Drakos
description: The Drakaina is a female serpent or dragon from Greek mythology, specifically the feminine form of the drakon, possessing both serpentine and human-like features that distinguish it from the more common male dragons of Hellenic tradition. In Greek mythological texts, the Drakaina appears as a sacred female serpent spirit that is typically slain only by gods or demigods rather than mortal heroes, reflecting her elevated status in the Greek mythological hierarchy. Notable examples of the Drakaina include Echidna, the mother of all monsters who mated with Typhon to produce Cerberus, the Hydra, the Chimera, and the Nemean Lion; Campe, the guardian of the Tartarus prison who was slain by Zeus; and Delphyne, the serpent who guarded the umbilical cord of Zeus and was killed by Apollo. The Drakaina represents the primordial, chthonic female power of the ancient Greek world, embodying the dangerous yet generative forces of the earth
source: Greek mythology, Hesiod & Homer

name: Draugar
description: Drakos is the modern Greek term for dragon, representing a rich tradition of dragon mythology that bridges ancient Hellenic dragon lore with the Christian-era folktales of Greece. In Greek folklore, particularly as catalogued in Georgios Megas's comprehensive Greek Folktale Catalogue, the Drakos appears as a common antagonist in hero tales, typically associated with mountains, caves, and hidden lairs where it guards princesses, treasure, or sacred springs. The Drakos tradition represents a continuous evolution from the ancient Greek drakonta, the serpentine monsters of classical mythology like the Lernaean Hydra and the Colchian Dragon, into the more anthropomorphized dragons of medieval and modern Greek folklore. These creatures serve as tests of heroism and cleverness, representing the obstacles that heroes must overcome to achieve marriage, wealth, or magical power, and they appear in countless variations across the Greek islands and mainland
source: Icelandic folklore, Íslenzkar þjóðsögur by Jón Árnason

name: Draugen
description: Draugar are the undead revenants of Icelandic folklore and Old Norse mythology, representing the animated corpses of the deceased who rise from their graves to haunt the living. Unlike ghosts or spectral apparitions, the Draugar are corporeal undead with physical, tangible bodies that possess superhuman strength and a malevolent intelligence. In the Icelandic sagas, which provide the earliest written accounts of these beings, the Draugar typically dwell within their burial mounds or travel to nearby farms, bringing disease, death, and misfortune to all who encounter them. The most famous Draugar in saga literature include Karr the Old in Grettis Saga and the vampire-like Glamr, whose curse plagued the hero Grettir for the rest of his life. The belief in Draugar was deeply embedded in Norse culture, where how people died and how they were buried directly affected whether they would become Draugar, with mean, greedy, or evil individuals being the most likely to rise again
source: Norse mythology; Draugar are undead spirits of the dead, documented in the Sagas and Nordic folklore.

name: Draugr (Swedish variant)
description: The Swedish variant of the Draugr shares many characteristics with its Norse cousins but has developed distinct features shaped by Sweden's unique coastal geography and maritime traditions. In Swedish folklore, the Draugr, also known regionally as drög or draug, is specifically associated with the Baltic Sea coast and the archipelagoes of Sweden, where it appears as the undead spirit of sailors and fishermen who died at sea. The Swedish Draugr tradition emphasizes the creature's role as both a guardian of sunken treasure and a bringer of storms, reflecting the dual nature of the Baltic Sea as both a source of livelihood and a cause of death for coastal communities. Unlike the more varied Draugr of Icelandic sagas, the Swedish variant is almost exclusively maritime in nature, with strong connections to shipwrecks, fishing disasters, and the treasures that lie beneath the waves In Iceland folklore, this figure is known among the Iceland people.
source: Norse mythology; draugar are corporeal undead, documented in the Sagas and Norse ethnographic studies.

name: Eloko
description: Eloko is a spirit from Mongo-Nkundo mythology. These forest-dwelling creatures are believed to be the restless spirits of ancestors who died with unresolved grudges, condemned to haunt the darkest, densest parts of the rainforest. Unlike benevolent spirits, the Eloko are fiercely territorial and vengeful, guarding their forest treasures including game animals and rare plants. They are known to cast spells on trespassers using enchanted bells that paralyze their victims before they attack. The Eloko embody the Mongo-Nkundo belief that the dead can return to settle scores with the living, serving as both a warning to honor one's ancestors and a caution against exploiting forest resources without proper respect. They share similarities with other Central African forest spirits such as the Sasabonsam of Ghana In Democratic Republic of the Congo folklore, this figure is known among the Mongo-Nkundo people.
source: Mongo-Nkundo oral tradition

name: Kakungu
description: Kakungu is a powerful ancestral spirit of the Suku people of southwestern Democratic Republic of Congo, regarded as the most authoritative figure in the mukanda initiation tradition. Far more than a ceremonial mask or ritual prop, Kakungu is believed to embody an actual ancestral spirit whose presence oversees the transition of boys into adulthood. Entering ritual spaces as a guardian, healer, and symbol of continuity between the living and their ancestors, Kakungu is perceived by the community as an active spiritual being entrusted with the power to protect, discipline, and restore balance. During initiation seasons, the Suku do not see Kakungu as a performer but as the literal embodiment of their most powerful ancestor. His role includes safeguarding initiates during circumcision rites, warding off malevolent forces, and ensuring the survival of those undergoing the symbolic journey of death and rebirth. The name 'Kakungu' refers both to the spirit and the giant mask that represents him
source: Suku oral tradition and ethnographic studies

name: Mokele-Mbembe
description: Mokele-Mbembe is a dragon from Bantu mythology. This cryptid is described as a large, reptilian creature resembling a sauropod dinosaur with a long, flexible neck and a single horn or tooth. Stories of the creature have been told for centuries among the Bantu peoples of Central Africa, including the Ba'Aka, whose oral traditions speak of a beast that lurks in deep river pools and swamps. During the early 20th century, European explorers and cryptozoologists brought the legend to global attention, leading to over fifty expeditions searching for evidence. While most scientists believe the stories stem from misidentified rhinoceroses, large snakes, or folk memory of once-extant megafauna, the mokele-mbembe remains one of Africa's most famous cryptids. In recent years, deforestation and habitat loss have led to increased reported sightings as displaced wildlife is mistaken for the legendary creature In Democratic Republic of the Congo folklore, this figure is known among the Bantu (multiple groups including Lingala, Ba'Aka) people.
source: Bantu/Lingala oral tradition and cryptozoological literature

name: Obrigwabibikwa
description: Obrigwabibikwa is a mystical dwarf and shapeshifter from the mythology of the Mbuti Pygmy people of the Democratic Republic of Congo. This enigmatic figure possesses the ability to transform into a reptile, most commonly a lizard, which holds sacred significance in Mbuti cosmology. The lizard is considered the divine messenger of Khonvoum, the supreme creator god of the Mbuti, who uses these creatures to communicate with the mortal world. Obrigwabibikwa plays a crucial role in Mbuti beliefs about death and the soul: when a person dies, their soul (megbe) splits into two parts, with one part inhabiting a totem animal. If the totem is killed or the son fails to inhale the megbe, the soul becomes a wandering spirit. Obrigwabibikwa is said to be responsible for creating these wandering spirits, making him a figure associated with the forces of order and chaos
source: Mbuti oral tradition

name: Drekavac
description: The Drekavac, meaning 'the screamer' or 'the screecher,' is a terrifying mythical creature from South Slavic mythology, with particularly strong belief in Bosnia and Herzegovina. It is most commonly described as the restless spirit of an unbaptized child that rises from its grave at night to haunt the living, emitting horrifying wails that blend animal cries with human sobs. In Maglaj, Bosnia, it takes the form of ghostly fallen soldiers unable to find peace, while in Kozarska Dubica it resembles a vampire-like undead man. The creature appears variably as a dappled, spindle-thin being with an oversized head, a humanoid canine, or a formless apparition. Its defining trait is its agonizing scream, which foretells death when appearing as a child or cattle disease when in animal form. The Drekavac is visible mainly at night, especially during the twelve days of Christmas (called 'unbaptized days') and early spring, and is repelled by dogs and bright light In Bosnia and Herzegovina folklore, this figure is known among the South Slavic (Bosnian, Serbian, Croatian) people.
source: Wikipedia, Crazy Alchemist Bestiary, Monstropedia, Radio Sarajevo, Your Guide to Bosnia

Its defining trait is its agonizing scream, which foretells death when appearing as a child or cattle disease when in animal form. The Drekavac is visible mainly at night, especially during the twelve days of Christmas (called 'unbaptized days') and early spring, and is repelled by dogs and bright light
source: Serbian folklore — Drekavac spirit documented in Serbian oral tradition.

name: Dreq
description: Dreq is a vampiric dragon-demon from Albanian folklore, a terrifying creature that rises from lakes and freshwater bodies to attack livestock and humans with relentless ferocity. The name Dreq derives from the Latin word draco meaning dragon or serpent, reflecting the ancient cultural exchanges between the Illyrian ancestors of the Albanians and the Roman Empire. In Albanian mythological tradition, the Dreq is closely related to the kulshedra, a multi-headed water serpent, but is distinguished by its more draconic form and vampiric tendencies. The Dreq is deeply embedded in Albanian folk beliefs about water spirits and their dangerous interactions with humans, serving as an explanation for drownings, livestock disappearances, and mysterious deaths near lakes and rivers throughout the Albanian countryside
source: Albanian folklore — Dreq dragon documented in Albanian oral tradition.

name: Druk (Thunder Dragon of Bhutan)
description: The Druk (Thunder Dragon) is the national symbol of Bhutan and a central figure in Bhutanese mythology and identity. The name Druk (from Dzongkha 'འབྲུག') means 'thunder dragon' and is the origin of Bhutan's name — Druk Yul ('Land of the Thunder Dragon'). According to legend, the Druk was first heard in the 12th century when the Tibetan Buddhist master Tsangpa Gyare Yeshe Dorje was establishing the Drukpa Kagyu school. While building the Ralung Monastery in Tibet, he heard a thunderous roar that sounded like a dragon's call three times. Interpreting this as an auspicious omen, he named his lineage Drukpa (the Dragon School). When the Drukpa Kagyu tradition was brought to Bhutan by Pema Lingpa and later established by Ngawang Namgyel (the Zhabdrung Rinpoche) in the 17th century, Bhutan became known as Druk Yul. The Druk represents power, strength, and the protective roar of thunder that clears away evil forces. It is believed to reside in the high mountains and to control the storms. The dragon's roar is the thunder, and its long, serpentine body is the lightning that splits the sky. The Druk is prominently displayed on Bhutan's national flag — a white dragon holding jewels against an orange and yellow background
source: Drukpa Kagyu tradition, Bhutanese national history, Pema Lingpa's terma revelations

name: Duende (Forest Guardian)
description: Duende (Forest Guardian) is a spirit from Belize mythology. Peruvian Duende traditions blend indigenous Quechua and Aymara beliefs with Spanish colonial influences, creating a rich and complex figure that varies significantly across Peru's three distinct geographical regions. In the Amazonian region of Peru, the Duende is closely related to the chullachaqui of indigenous lore, a shapeshifting forest spirit that protects the jungle and its creatures. In the Andean highlands, the Duende takes on characteristics of mountain spirits and earth guardians, watching over the campos and rural communities. The Peruvian Duende tradition plays a vital role in teaching environmental stewardship and respect for the natural world, particularly in indigenous communities where the forest is both a source of livelihood and a sacred space
source: Regional survey of Mesoamerican indigenous traditions — Maya, Aztec, Mixtec, Zapotec, and related peoples as documented in codices, ethnographies by Sahagún, Landa, and contemporary folklore collections.

name: Duizendpoot
description: The Duende of Belize is a prominent figure in the folklore of this Central American nation, where it represents the guardian spirit of the country's rich tropical forests, jungles, and wilderness areas. Belizean Duende traditions draw from both the Maya heritage of the region, particularly the Q'eqchi' and Mopan Maya peoples, and the mestizo and Creole cultural influences that have shaped Belize's unique identity. In Belizean folklore, the Duende is considered one of the most important supernatural beings of the forest, serving as the enforcer of traditional ecological knowledge and the protector of the natural resources that Belizean communities depend upon for their survival. The Belizean Duende is particularly active in the dense jungles of the Maya Mountains and the extensive cave systems that dot the Belizean landscape, where he guards both the natural treasures of the forest and the sacred Maya sites hidden within
source: Dutch folklore — beast documented in Dutch oral tradition.

name: Dullahan
description: Headless Rider - Irish 'Dubhlachan' (from dubh 'black'). Also called 'Colainn Gan Cheann' (body without head). NOT related to the Banshee (her lineage): the Dullahan is a solitary death Bringer, NOT a herald. The Banshee Warnings before death, but the Dullahan Brings the death himself. No parents, no family - he's a force, not a person. Rides the 'Coiste Bodhar' (Soundless Death Coach) made from Coffins, Bones, Funerary remnants. The coach axle is Spine, wheel-spokes are thigh bones. He carries his own Severed Head under his arm as a lantern - the dead eyes glow like coals, the grin has razor's teeth. The head calls out names - wherever he Stops is where death occurs. He rides at night with Black Horse. Some versions: he rides headless horses, carries a whip made from human spine. NOT benevolent - he's 'Unseelie fairy' (malevolent). One name: 'Gan Ceann' = without head. Unlike the Banshee, sees Your death rather than announcing it - he is death itself, riding to collect souls
source: Irish folklore — the Dullahan headless horseman documented in Irish oral tradition.

name: Duppy
description: Duppy is the Kittitian term for a restless spirit or ghost, derived from the Akan word of West Africa. Kitts and Nevis folklore, duppies are the spirits of dead persons that linger in places they frequented during life, especially plantations and secluded areas. While generally mischievous or harmless, some duppies can be vengeful if wronged in life. They are known for causing unexplained noises, moving objects, appearing in dreams, and playing tricks on the living. The belief in duppies reflects a deep connection to ancestors and a recognition of their continued presence in the world. Kittitians traditionally avoid calling a person's name loudly at night, as a duppy might answer. Grave sites are adorned with personal belongings to comfort the duppy's spirit. The Mocko Jumbie stilt walker tradition counters duppies — the tall dancer's height allows him to see and ward off these spirits
source: Caribbean folklore — Duppy ghosts documented across Caribbean oral tradition.

name: Dvärg (Swedish)
description: Dvärgar (dwarves) are master smiths and craftspeople of Norse mythology and Swedish folklore, born from the blood of the primordial giant Ymir. In the Norse creation myth, maggots from Ymir's flesh were transformed into dwarves by the gods, and they dwell underground in Svartálfheim (also called Niðavellir, the Dark Fields). Four dwarves — Austri, Vestri, Norðri, and Suðri — hold up the four corners of the sky. Dwarves are renowned across the Nine Worlds for their unparalleled skill in metallurgy and magic, having forged the most powerful artifacts in Norse myth: Thor's hammer Mjölnir, Odin's spear Gungnir, Freyr's ship Skíðblaðnir, the golden boar Gullinbursti, and the multiplying ring Draupnir. In later Swedish folk belief, dvärgar merged with the broader category of underjordiska (underground dwellers), described as small, quiet people living under boulders or near ancient burial mounds, deeply connected to nature and highly territorial. They are described as pitch-black in appearance and turn to stone if exposed to daylight
source: Poetic Edda, Prose Edda

name: Dwen
description: The Dwen is a haunting figure in Saint Lucian folklore — the spirit of a child who died before baptism, condemned to wander the earth. Called Dwen in Saint Lucia (Douen in Trinidad and Dwenn in Grenada), these entities are characterized by backward-facing feet with heels to the front and knees also reversed. They have no faces — only a smooth surface where features should be, except for a small mouth to speak with. They wear large floppy straw hats to hide their facelessness. The Dwen is said to wait near forest edges and call to children by name, mimicking a parent's voice, trying to lure them into the woods. In Saint Lucian tradition, the Dwen is sometimes associated with Papa Bois and is considered a protector of the natural world. The legend reflects the historical importance of baptism in Saint Lucian society — dying unbaptized meant eternal restlessness
source: Saint Lucian oral tradition; snip Wikipedia (Douen); snip Sweettntmagazine

name: Eagle Animal-Spirit of Kwakiutl
description: The Eagle Animal-Spirit is a revered figure in Kwakiutl (Kwakwaka-wakw) mythology of the Pacific Northwest Coast, serving as a guardian of hills and elevated places within the traditional territories of Vancouver Island and the adjacent mainland of British Columbia. In Kwakiutl culture, the eagle is one of the four primary clans, alongside the Killer Whale, Raven, and Wolf, and holds significant ceremonial importance. Eagles are believed to be powerful ancestral spirits that can transform between human and animal forms, appearing in the intricate transformation masks used during potlatch ceremonies. The Eagle Animal-Spirit is associated with the Sky World, spiritual vision, and inherited family crest privileges that are passed down through generations within specific numaym (lineage groups)
source: Indigenous North American folk beliefs and ethnographic records, including academic studies of Native American spiritual traditions.

name: Eahpáraš
description: Eahpáraš is a restless, wandering spirit in Sami folklore — the soul of someone who died improperly, particularly children who died before being named, baptized, or properly integrated into the community. These spirits cannot transition to Jábmiidaibmu (the underworld) and are condemned to wander the earth, causing trouble for the living. They can cause illness, misfortune, or simply wail in the wilderness. The most tragic cases are murdered children whose spirits return to haunt their parents. The only remedy is to perform proper burial rites, even long after death, to allow the soul to find peace. The concept reflects the Sami belief that a proper death includes not only physical death but also proper social and spiritual transition. An eahpáraš is not inherently evil but is displaced and miserable — its mischief stems from its unresolved state. The phenomenon is extensively documented in Emilie Demant Hatt's By the Fire (1922) collection of Sami stories
source: Emilie Demant Hatt, By the Fire (1922); Sami Folktales from the Near and Far Worlds
